Secrete androgen-binding protein (ABP), which binds testosterone and keeps it highly concentrated in the tubules. Testosterone in the testis is higher than in the blood, and the developing sperm depend on that strong signal. 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone in the tissues that are more sensitive to DHT, which express a lot of the enzyme. The male sexual response is controlled by both divisions of the autonomic nervous system. Everything leading up to ejaculation, the erection and the lubrication, is parasympathetic; the climax, emission and ejaculation, is sympathetic. His mnemonic is "Point and Shoot": P for point, parasympathetic; S for shoot, sympathetic. "It's crude, but you'll remember it." 2 Sertoli versus Leydig cells: where each sits, FSH versus LH, what each makes (ABP, inhibin, aromatase, AMH versus testosterone) and the blood-testis barrier Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Make a two-column list and know it cold: Sertoli (tubule wall, FSH, nourishment, blood-testis barrier, ABP, inhibin, aromatase, spermiation, AMH in the fetus) against Leydig (interstitium, LH, testosterone). Form tight junctions with one another, creating the blood-testis barrier. The testis is an immune-privileged site: if immune cells got in, they could mount an autoreactive response against the haploid germ cells and damage them. Inhibin acts at the pituitary only; testosterone acts at both the hypothalamus (GnRH) and the pituitary (mainly LH). Inhibin, from the Sertoli cells, acts only at the anterior pituitary, where it turns off FSH, not LH. Asked in class, he was clear that inhibin doesn't feed back to the hypothalamus. (Testosterone's brake on GnRH lowers FSH too, indirectly.) When serum testosterone falls, GnRH and LH secretion rise; when it rises, they fall. These loops keep serum testosterone within a narrow range. His slide adds a point about timing: GnRH, and so LH, must be released in pulses to maintain normal testosterone production. Continuous GnRH does the opposite of what you might expect: it decreases LH secretion, and therefore decreases testosterone. Damaged tubules, healthy Leydig cells: inhibin falls, so FSH rises on its own, while LH and testosterone stay normal. 4 Aromatase: mostly in the Sertoli cells from fetal life on (his correction of the slide), turned up by FSH; testosterone to estradiol, androstenedione to estrone; what estradiol does in men Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Aromatase, also called estrogen synthase, converts testosterone into estradiol and androstenedione into estrone; estrone is the main source of estrogen after menopause (L16). The person is XY, so testes form, but no scrotum develops, so the testes stay inside the body and never descend. The Sertoli cells make AMH, which needs no androgen receptor, so the Müllerian ducts regress: there is no uterus and there are no ovaries. Testosterone and DHT have no working receptor, so the Wolffian ducts regress too. The external genitalia follow the default pathway and are female, with a blind-ended vagina, and the secondary sex characteristics are female: breast development and little body hair. The result is a person who is genetically XY and has testes, but looks female. 7 Point and shoot: erection and lubrication parasympathetic, emission and ejaculation sympathetic Flagged in the recording · 1 question in the bank Explained under 1 above: Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): FSH acts on Sertoli cells, androgen-binding protein holds testosterone high, emission is sympathetic; and their twins 8 Erection and sildenafil: NO dilates the cavernosal arteries, guanylate cyclase and cGMP, compressed veins, PDE5 blocked Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Nitric oxide from parasympathetic nerves dilates the cavernosal arteries; the engorged tissue then compresses the veins. NO activates guanylate cyclase and raises cGMP; sildenafil blocks PDE5 so cGMP stays high. The penis is mostly spongy, cavernous connective tissue: the corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum. The vessels to remember are the cavernosal arteries, which drive the erection. During sexual arousal the parasympathetic nerves fire, and their postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine and nitric oxide. Nitric oxide is the key: it dilates the cavernosal arteries, more blood flows into the spongy tissue, and the tissue engorges. The engorged tissue then compresses the veins that drain it, so the blood can't drain out, and the result is an erection. At the molecular level, nitric oxide activates the enzyme guanylate cyclase, which converts GTP into cyclic GMP, or cGMP. As cGMP rises, the arterial smooth muscle relaxes, the vessels dilate, and everything above follows. cGMP is normally broken down quickly by phosphodiesterase type 5, PDE5, which ends the signal. 9 Spermatogenesis and the sperm: the cell sequence, four haploid spermatids, the acrosome and midpiece, maturation in the epididymis Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this The acrosome comes from the Golgi and carries the enzymes that get the sperm through the egg's layers; the midpiece's mitochondria power the tail. The spermatozoa released into the tubule are not functional yet: they can't move and can't fertilize. Maturation is completed in the epididymis. About 18 to 24 hours after sperm enter it, signals there (enzymes and growth factors from the epididymis's cells and fluid) let them start to gain motility and the ability to fertilize. His slide adds that they lose cytoplasm and acquire forward motility proteins and acrosomal stabilizing factors. Sperm are also stored in the epididymis, for up to several months. Dr. Herr's histology lecture gives 2 to 12 days for maturation in the epididymis; this lecture's 18 to 24 hours is when the change begins. Acrosome: the cap at the very top of the head, a specialized vacuole formed from the Golgi apparatus. It holds hyaluronidase and proteolytic enzymes that let the sperm penetrate the layers that protect the egg (more on those layers in L16 and L17). 10 Making testosterone: Leydig cells, LH, cholesterol desmolase (rate-limiting), adrenal androgens; testosterone across life Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Testosterone is a steroid hormone: the Leydig cells make it from cholesterol in response to LH. LH stimulates the expression and activity of cholesterol desmolase, the P450 side-chain cleavage enzyme, the key regulated step; it's the same step ACTH controls in the adrenal cortex. His slide calls it the rate-limiting step. The weak adrenal androgens, DHEA and androstenedione, can also be funneled into this pathway, so the Leydig cells can turn them into testosterone (and in women, they feed the female sex hormones, L16). His slide traces testosterone with age, and he walked through it. Testosterone is high during gestation, building the male structures; it peaks again soon after birth; then it goes quiet through childhood. It surges at puberty and stays fairly steady through adulthood: it has peaks and valleys, but it isn't cyclic the way the female hormones are. In old age it declines. That decline is multifactorial and still not fully understood: sometimes the Leydig cells stop responding to LH as they should, sometimes the problem is at the hypothalamus. His slide notes call the gradual decline late-onset hypogonadism, or age-related low testosterone. 11 The accessory glands: seminal vesicles 60 to 70 percent (fructose, prostaglandins, the fibrinogen clot), prostate 20 to 30 percent (PSA breaks the clot), Cowper's lubrication; temperature, 34 degrees Celsius Flagged in the recording · 5 questions in the bank Seminal vesicles: secretory glands that make about 60 to 70 percent of the seminal fluid (his slide says 50 to 80; Dr. Herr's histology lecture, about 70). Their fluid has fructose, which the sperm metabolize for the energy to swim, citric acid and other nutrients. It has prostaglandins, which, once the semen is in the female reproductive tract, stimulate contractions of the tract that help the sperm move. And it has fibrinogen and other clotting factors: soon after ejaculation the semen clots, which keeps the sperm in the female tract longer. The fluid is somewhat alkaline. During ejaculation the seminal vesicle empties into the ejaculatory duct. Seminal vesicles Fructose, citric acid, prostaglandins, fibrinogen 60 to 70 percent of the fluid; energy for sperm; contractions of the female tract; the clot that holds sperm there Prostate Thin, milky fluid: citrate, phosphate, calcium; PSA 20 to 30 percent; neutralizes acidity; PSA breaks down the clot Bulbourethral (Cowper's) Clear, thick mucus, before ejaculation Lubricates and neutralizes the urethra Also flagged in class AMH from the Sertoli cells makes the Müllerian ducts regress; without it, a uterus forms. It works even in androgen insensitivity, which is why neither disorder has a uterus. Leydig cells, in the interstitium, make testosterone from cholesterol under LH. If a question asks where aromatase is, answer the Sertoli cells (turned up by FSH) at every age, not the Leydig cells his slide names for adults. FSH goes with Sertoli and LH with Leydig; both receptors are Gs-coupled and work through PKA. Know the cell order (spermatogonia, primary and secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa), four haploid spermatids with 23 chromosomes each, and that maturation finishes in the epididymis. Use 34 degrees Celsius for this lecture (Dr. Herr's L13 says about 35); warm, the testes hang lower, cold, the scrotum tightens and pulls them up.
